items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I was there with bells on because Smittie had told me what a great horn player Joe Smith was and I didn't want to miss hearing one note. ... Suddenly Joe Smith was on the band stand blowing that sweet sound that I had never heard anyone play before.

ctx.x: We did quite a few dance jobs for the Elks at their hall and some dance jobs at the only negro hotel on Walnut Hills. Naturally we all felt very proud to be able to play for dancers. But we were not learning to read very well and John Coleman could not read at all. Nevertheless we had our repertoire and enjoyed playing our solos the best that we could.

William Smith the pianist was now playing with Clarence Page but I was at his house quite often. The Chocolate Dandies show came to one of the theatres up town and with them was a trumpet player featured in the show by the name of Joe Smith. William Smith met Joe Smith and invited him to come to his house for a session one night after the show. I was there with bells on because Smittie had told me what a great horn player Joe Smith was and I didn't want to miss hearing one note. I don't remember if Joe drank…

One night during the stay of the Chocolate Dandies (shows of that type usually stayed for one month in Cincy) there was a dance at the Sterling Hotel and Clarence Page's orchestra was playing. I had been to a rehearsal and decided to stop in the Sterling Hotel and listen for a while. I put my horn on the band stand and stood there listening and watching the dancers. Suddenly Joe Smith was on the band stand blowing that sweet sound that I had never heard anyone play before. After a certain time, I wanted to leave,…

items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I never moved from the place I had in front of the band until they played the last number of the afternoon... and the three Smith brothers, Luc, Joe and Russell

ctx.x: The band came a day before they were to play and I remember the first one I saw but I didn't know, was Russell Smith. My instinct told me that he was from New York because he was dressed so well, and no-one around town had the class he had. So I asked him if he was the band and he told me yes. I told him that I would be at the dance because it was on a Sunday and they were playing that afternoon and night at the Crystal Ballroom which was at 5th and Plum Street.

I was there that afternoon before the band played their first number and I never moved from the place I had in front of the band until they played the last number of the afternoon. Joe Smith was the only one that had been in Cincinnati before and it was the first time to see Coleman Hawkins, Buster Bailey, Don Redman, "Big" Green, Charlie Dixon, banjo, Kaiser Marshall, drums, Bobby Escudero, tuba, Fletcher himself and the three Smith brothers, Luc, Joe and Russell - known as "Rops".

Fletcher played most of the songs I had heard him play on records and many I had never heard, but the thing that amazed me mostly was that "Big" Green usually took his solos after Joe Smith who was the only trumpet soloist for the jumping numbers in the band, and Green played note for note everything that Joe played. Joe's solos were played sweet in the Joe Smith style, and there were no solos on trumpet the way Armstrong had played "Money Blues".
